draft.title: Issues in the media
card: An issue is a topic that people disagree about. Reasonable people can hold different views on it.
Issues are debated in many places: news reports, opinion pieces, speeches, podcasts and social media posts.
A fact is not an issue, because it is not in dispute. A question such as whether phones should be banned in schools is an issue, because people answer it differently.
When you read an argument, first name the issue. This tells you what the debate is about before you look at the writer's view.
draft.remember: An issue is a topic with more than one reasonable view, argued in many kinds of media.

a.q: Which of these is an issue?
opts: Whether councils should ban cars from city centres
The number of trams that run in Melbourne
The date a new library opened in Ballarat
The height of a bridge over the Yarra
a.why: People can reasonably disagree about banning cars, so it is an issue. The other three are facts that can be looked up, so nobody is arguing about them.
a.clue: Which one could two sensible people argue about?

b.q: A podcast host in Geelong spends an episode arguing that teenagers should be allowed to vote at 16. What is the issue?
opts: Whether the voting age should be lowered to 16
Whether podcasts are a good way to share ideas
How many teenagers live in Geelong
When the next election will be held
b.why: The issue is the topic people disagree on: the voting age. A podcast is only the place where the debate happens, so the second option confuses the medium with the issue.
b.clue: Name the topic being argued, not the place it is argued.

a.best: Whether councils should ban cars from city centres

b.best: Whether the voting age should be lowered to 16

problems.detail: Why (b) refers to 'the second option' as confusing the medium with the issue, but options are shown in random order. The podcast option may not be second (here it is fourth), so name the option instead of its position.

The right option is the only one framed as a 'Whether...' question, matching the card's 'a question such as whether...'. The other three are noun phrases, so a student could pick it from its form alone. Consider phrasing some distractors as questions too.

check.summary: The card and both answers are correct. Why (b) refers to an option by position ('the second option'), which breaks when options are shuffled. In question a, the right option is the only one phrased as a 'Whether...' question, which gives it away.
